newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed after smallish U.S.trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed after smallish U.S.trade gap.

text.p: The dollar ended higher against the yen, getting a lift after the Commerce Department reported a smaller than expected U.S. trade deficit in April.
But the dollar fell against the German currency, after yen selling vaulted mark/yen over 66.00 in New York.

Short covering boosted the dollar almost one yen after the government reported that the trade gap in April was $8.36 billion, well below the $10 billion shortfall priced into the market but still larger than the downwardly-revised $7.76 billion in March.

The rise came despite a 5.1 percent increase in the politically-touchy deficit with Japan, which was expected to be a topic of discussion when the leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations gather Friday in Denver.
"It seems to be a late burst of short-covering in front of this G7," said Bob Near, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Bank of New York.

"Maybe alot of people were changing their minds," Near continued. "We're not going to expect anything out of it that's going to put any heat on the Japanese surplus. That's what the markets seem to be telling us."
The dollar ended at 114.06/11 yen, up from 113.32/42 at the open but fell to 1.7235/45 marks from 1.7300/10.
Earlier this year the dollar advanced to multiyear highs, prompting forecasts that U.S. exports, priced in dollars, would become uncompetitive overseas.
These fears were borne out to some degree on Wednesday when Japan reported that its surplus with the United States nearly doubled in May.
But Marc Chandler, a senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said that trade does not affect the dollar against the yen as much as it used to.
"The Japanese have restructured their economy and they are becoming less dependent on the U.S. as a market for their exports," he said, adding Japan is now more focused on southeastAsian markets.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, in a White House interview recorded with Japanese television before departing for Denver on Thursday, said he was concerned about Japan's large surplus with the United States but said exchange rates should not be used as a way to correct trade imbalances.
Elsewhere, the dollar was also pressured after weekly jobless claims data fueled bets that the Federal Reserve would not increase interest rates at its next policy-setting meeting on July 1-2.

A report on Thursday showed a jump of 8,000 in the number of Americans filing for unemployment benefits last week, leading analysts to expect a weak April employment number from the Labor Department in two weeks.
The dollar was hurt by the claims data but shook off a stronger-than-expected Philadelphia Fed business activity index, which stood at 25.2 in June compared to 1.6 in May.

"Blend that in and that's why we're seeing a little more dollar weakness against sterling and dollar weakness against marks, whereas yen is sort of definately a trade issue," said David Durrant, senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc.
The dollar fell to 1.4382/92 Swiss francs from 1.4454/59 andto Canadian $1.3874/79 from C$1.3916/21.
The pound rose to $1.6485/95 from $1.6415/25 and the Australian dollar rose to $0.7500/05 from $0.7488/93.
